title: 27. Linux Security & Hardening
content:
# 27. Linux Security & Hardening

Linux security work is a balance of least privilege, patching, auditability, and operational practicality. Hardening should reduce risk without making systems unmaintainable.

## Learning goals

By the end of this module, you should be able to:

- inspect users, groups, sudo access, and file permissions;
- reason about services running with least privilege;
- identify common SSH and secret-handling risks;
- understand patching and exposure reduction;
- make hardening changes with verification and rollback.

## Users, groups, and sudo

```bash
id appuser
getent passwd appuser
getent group sudo
sudo -l
```

Review who can become root and how. Prefer named users and groups over shared accounts. Use sudo rules that grant the minimum command access required.

## File permissions

```bash
stat /etc/app/config.env
namei -l /etc/app/config.env
find /srv/app -type f -perm -0002 -print
```

World-writable files and overly broad secret permissions are common findings. For secrets, start with owner-only access unless the service model requires otherwise.

## Service privileges

Inspect systemd units:

```bash
systemctl cat api.service
systemctl show api.service --property=User,Group,NoNewPrivileges,ProtectSystem,PrivateTmp
```

A service should usually run as a dedicated non-root user. systemd sandboxing options can reduce filesystem, network, and privilege exposure, but test them carefully against application needs.

## SSH posture

Check effective SSH server configuration:

```bash
sshd -T | sort
```

Common goals include key-based authentication, limited root login, reasonable idle behavior, and clear ownership of authorized keys. Do not lock out your only access path; keep a tested recovery session when changing SSH.

## Patching and inventory

Security depends on knowing what runs:

```bash
uname -a
cat /etc/os-release
systemctl --type=service --state=running
ss -lntup
```

Use the distribution package manager for security updates and track exceptions. Emergency patching should still include validation and rollback planning.

## Network exposure

```bash
ss -lntup
```

Every listening socket should have an owner and a reason. If a service only needs local access, bind it to `127.0.0.1` or a private interface instead of all interfaces.

## Secrets

Avoid secrets in command lines, shell history, Git, logs, and process listings. Prefer secret managers, restricted environment files, stdin prompts, or platform-native secret injection. If a secret leaks, rotate it; deleting the visible copy is not enough.

## Audit mindset

A useful security review records:

- asset and owner;
- exposure;
- current control;
- risk;
- recommended change;
- verification;
- rollback.

## Practice

Review a disposable Linux host or container. Identify one excessive permission, one unnecessary listener, one service privilege improvement, and one secret-handling risk. Apply one safe fix and document how you verified it.
